lesson.title: Standardization: Putting Every Distribution on the Same Scale
lesson.summary: Standardization is the process of converting every value in a data set into a z-score, producing a new set of values that always has a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1, regardless of the original units or shape.
lesson.body:
Standardization takes the z-score formula and applies it to an entire data set at once, not just a single value. Every observation x is replaced by its z-score, x minus mean, divided by standard deviation. The result is a new list of standardized values, often called z-values, that describes exactly the same relative pattern as the original data but strips away the original units and the original scale entirely.

This process always produces two guaranteed properties, no matter what the original data looked like. First, the mean of the standardized values is always exactly 0. Second, the standard deviation of the standardized values is always exactly 1. These are not coincidences specific to one data set; they follow directly from how mean and standard deviation respond to a linear transformation like subtracting a constant and dividing by another constant, so the result holds for any data set you standardize.

Standardize the familiar data set 4, 8, 6, 5, and 3, using its mean of 5.2 and standard deviation of approximately 1.9235. The five z-values work out to approximately -0.62, 1.46, 0.42, -0.10, and -1.14. Adding these five z-values gives a sum extremely close to 0, with any tiny deviation from exactly 0 explained by rounding the individual values, confirming that the standardized mean is 0. This will happen for any data set you standardize, because subtracting the mean before dividing is precisely what forces the new values to balance around 0.

Standardization is what makes it meaningful to compare values that started out in completely different units or on completely different scales, something raw numbers alone can never do. A height in centimeters and a weight in kilograms cannot be directly compared, but their z-scores can, because both have been converted onto the same standardized scale of number of standard deviations from the mean of their own distribution. This is also why standardization matters so much for combining or comparing variables in more advanced statistical methods, where mixing raw units would make no sense, and why fields as different as finance, medicine, and education all rely on some version of standardized scoring to put unlike measurements on common footing.

One important limitation to remember is that standardizing a distribution does not change its shape, only its location and scale. A strongly skewed distribution is still just as skewed after standardization; it simply has a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1 instead of its original mean and standard deviation, and any outliers in the original data are still outliers, now expressed as z-values with unusually large magnitudes. Standardization recenters and rescales a distribution, but it does not fix problems like skewness or outliers, which is why the cautions about interpreting z-scores in skewed data still apply fully to standardized data.
